html:
A network of lunchbox couriers in Mumbai who carry home-cooked meals from people's homes to their workplaces and bring the empty boxes back the same day. The service began around 1890.

Tradition says it started when a man named Mahadeo Havaji Bachche began delivering lunch to office workers in Bombay, a city of long commutes and workers who wanted food from home. It grew into an association of several thousand carriers, most from farming families of the Pune region, who share earnings as members rather than employees.

Each box passes through several hands. It is picked up by bicycle, sorted at a station, carried on the city's suburban trains, sorted again and delivered by noon. Most dabbawalas had little schooling, so the system uses a simple code of letters, numbers and colours painted on the lids. Its reputation for almost never losing or misdelivering a box has made it a favourite case study for business schools around the world. It depends on the dense local railway that grew from the first train in India, which ran out of Bombay in 1853.
